problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=x(3+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+2{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}.
$$

If ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ then general solution can be expressed in parametric form $(x(t),y(t)),$ where

$$
x(t)=C{e}^{-t/3}+f(t)
$$

and $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Find the function $f(t).$

*Hint: Under the given transformation, we have*

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{3}x=-\frac{4}{3}t.
$$

*You may also wish to make use of the following result (constants omitted):*

$$
\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t=(t-1){e}^{t}
$$

feedback.problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=x{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}).
$$

If ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ then general solution can be expressed in parametric form $(x(t),y(t)),$ where

$$
y(t)=(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C}{(1-t)^{2}})f(t)+g(t)
$$

and $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Find $f(t)+g(t).$

*Hint: Under the given transformation, we have*

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2x}{t-1}=\frac{1}{t(1-t)}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

We're told that, under the substitution ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2x}{t-1}=\frac{1}{t(1-t)}
$$

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

we compute our integrating factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int P(t)\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2/(t-1)\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|t-1|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-1)^{2}} \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our differential equation by $I(t)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(t-1)^{2}\frac{2x}{t-1}=(t-1)^{2}\frac{1}{t(1-t)} \\ (t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(t-1)x=-(t-1)^{2}\frac{1}{t(t-1)} \\ (t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(t-1)x=-\frac{t-1}{t} \\ (t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(t-1)x=\frac{1-t}{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x(t-1)^{2}) & =\frac{1-t}{t} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x(t-1)^{2})\,\text{d}t & =\int \frac{1-t}{t}\,\text{d}t \\ x(t-1)^{2} & =\int \frac{1}{t}-1\,\text{d}t \\ x(t-1)^{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C}{(t-1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
x(t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C}{(t-1)^{2}}.
$$

To recover $y$, we substitute $x$ into

$$
y=x{t}^{2}+t,
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C}{(t-1)^{2}}){t}^{2}+t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $f(t)={t}^{2},g(t)=t,$ and

$$
f(t)+g(t)={t}^{2}+t.
$$
